reasons: Lake identity gives case_name California v. Hodari D., court U.S. Supreme Court, year 1991, and date_decided 1991-04-23.
Lake citations list official citation 499 U.S. 621, the asserted parallel citations, and the asserted vendor-neutral citations.
Opinion text header confirms 499 U.S. 621 (1991), Supreme Court of the United States, and decided April 23, 1991.
The opinion frames the issue as whether Hodari had been seized when he dropped the drugs, and says if not, the drugs were abandoned and lawfully recovered.

At star page 626 the opinion says: "The narrow question before us is whether, with respect to a show of authority as with respect to application of physical force, a seizure occurs even though the subject does not yield. We hold that it does not."
The opinion adds that an arrest requires physical force or, absent that, submission to authority.
The conclusion states that because Hodari did not comply, he was not seized until tackled, and the cocaine abandoned while running was not the fruit of a seizure.
residual_risks: The holding should not be read to cover facts where physical force or submission occurred before the contraband was discarded.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: State the second clause as: contraband discarded while fleeing before physical force or submission is not the fruit of a seizure.

reasons: The opinion expressly addresses seizure of the person under the Fourth Amendment.
The case refines Terry and Mendenhall by holding that a show of authority alone does not complete a seizure without submission.
The Supreme Court merits holding on when a person is seized supports the home role as a key refinement under Seizure of the Person.
residual_risks: The exact label "Key" is editorial, but the disclosed opinion supports the classification.
